headline: Forced labour guidelines published; ESMA details 2026 sustainability reporting priorities
summary: The European Commission published official guidelines for the Forced Labour Regulation, carrying significant implications for Chinese supply chains. Simultaneously, EU bodies detailed sustainability enforcement priorities and proposed caps on supplier data burdens. Member states also intensified debates over potential ETS2 implementation delays.

items.title: Commission publishes EU Forced Labour Regulation guidelines
items.what: The European Commission has published official implementation guidelines detailing how competent authorities will apply the EU Forced Labour Regulation across import supply chains.
items.meaning: As an EU brand importing finished tools from China, you face structured enforcement scrutiny regarding labour practices and component traceability across your supplier network.
items.action: Benchmark current Chinese factory audit protocols and supply chain traceability against the newly published Commission guidelines.

sources.title: Update on the EU Forced Labour Regulation: The European Commission's Guidelines Have Been Published

items.title: Data limits reported for sustainability requests to mid-sized suppliers
items.what: Rules were reported establishing data ceilings that permit suppliers with up to 1,000 employees to refuse excessive sustainability data requests from corporate buyers.
items.meaning: Your Chinese and component suppliers may legally resist bespoke sustainability questionnaires, complicating the Scope 3 and social data collection required for your CSRD reporting.
items.action: Rationalise supplier data requests to align strictly with standard ESRS datapoints, avoiding custom inquiries that invite refusal.

sources.title: Brussels Sets a Data Ceiling: Suppliers With Up to 1,000 Staff Can Now Refuse Extra Sustainability R

items.title: ESMA establishes 2026 priorities for sustainability reporting enforcement
items.what: ESMA issued its 2026 enforcement priorities, focusing strictly on double materiality determinations and connectivity between sustainability statements and financial disclosures.
items.meaning: National regulators will examine whether your CSRD reporting demonstrates verifiable double materiality logic and consistent integration with published financial figures.
items.action: Ensure your double materiality assessment documentation explicitly ties supplier-related ESG risks to financial accounting impacts.
